title: The Healer's Blessed Hands
hookLine: a Vedic healer blesses their own two hands, and Hindus still greet the divine in their palms each morning
carry: the sacred is in your hands: see them first
tomorrow: what do Hindu families chant for someone who's sick?
last: NAMAH: BOW, THEN ASK IT TO PASS.

lines: A HYMN SPEAKS TO THE HANDS.
cards: A hand on a forehead. It's the check that comes before any thermometer. Someone leans over a sick child, lays a palm there, and the hand asks a question: hot, or not?
But something else happens too. The child's shoulders drop a little. Somebody is here.
The hand is part of the answer before anyone knows what the answer is.
One healing hymn in the Atharva Veda ends right at that spot: not with an herb, not with a potion, but with the healer looking down at their own two hands and speaking to them.

teach.h: RAISE UP THE ONE WHO FELL.
teach.b: The Atharva Veda keeps hymns for the bedside, and one of them, in its fourth book, opens with a plea: you gods, raise up again the one who has fallen.
Then the healer turns, not to the patient and not to a god, but to their own hands. In paraphrase: this hand of mine is blessed.

teach.h: THIS HAND BLESSED, THIS ONE MORE BLESSED.
teach.b: This other hand is more blessed still. This one holds every remedy, vishvabheshaja, all-healing. This one's touch is kind.

And then: with these two hands of ten branches, and with the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands, we touch you. Hands and voice together, and the hands themselves called holy.
That idea didn't stay in the Veda.
Many Hindus begin every day with a short Sanskrit prayer called kara darshan, seeing the hands.

Before the phone, before the floor, you look into your open palms and say: at the fingertips lives Lakshmi, Goddess of plenty; in the middle, Saraswati, Goddess of learning; at the base, Govinda, Krishna.

Families say it a little differently, but the teaching is the same: the hands that will cook, write, work and care today are a home for the divine. An elder's blessing, too, comes as a hand on the head.
So the hands you bring to a sickbed, or to a sink full of dishes, aren't just tools.
In this tradition, they're where the day's work becomes worship.

how: Many Hindus begin the day with kara darshan, looking into their palms and naming Lakshmi, Saraswati and Govinda; elders bless with a hand on the head; Vedic verses for the sick are kept in recitation learned from a teacher.

games.q: what does “the atharva veda's healing hymns” mean?
o: a later handbook listing herbs and their exact doses
Vedic verses for the sick and for those who heal them
hymns kept for funerals and for honoring the dead

games.q: a heavy day is waiting: a sick grandparent, a test, a long shift. by the hymn and kara darshan, what do you do first?
o: check your phone for what went wrong overnight
look into your palms and greet the divine in them
keep your hands still so they can't do anything wrong
games.why: the healer blessed their own hands before touching the sick. kara darshan starts the day the same way: these hands are a home for the divine, so their work is worship.

practice: Open your hands in front of you, palms up, the way many Hindus do on waking. Look at the fingertips, then the middle of the palms, then the base, near the wrist.

If you pray, say the names as you go, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Govinda, and offer what these hands will do today. If you don't, simply look, and think of one person your hands will care for before the day is out.

wordCard.voice: The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, a healer's two blessed hands, and the morning prayer that still greets the divine in them.

orig.note: Sanskrit: all-healing, holding every remedy. Atharva Veda 4.13.6 says it of a hand.

carryVoice: Your line: the sacred is in your hands: see them first. One hand blessed, one more blessed still. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Atharva Veda 4.13.6–7 (this hand blessed, this one more blessed, holding every remedy, kind of touch; two hands of ten branches and the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands we touch you)
